about: Parisius (Paris, with the abbey and fair of Saint-Denis): one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/parisius.md and the spine. A draft for the user to overwrite.
woven: Woven with Quentovic, Rotomagus, Namnetis, Herio and Burdigala on 6 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways, parisius.aimoin made real (the monk of Saint-Germain whom the Rotomagus file's Einold and this file's Abbo named), beats placed across the region and the port's cards (encounters/neustria_west_793.json) put on their sites. Nothing was taken out.

ports.summary: Parisius is two places two hours' walk apart: an old Roman city on an island in the Seine, the seat of a bishop and a count, and the abbey of Saint Denis to the north, which a boat from the sea reaches first because the river loops. In 793 no king lives here; the abbey is the great house, and its fair, which opens on Saint Denis's day, is where the men from over the sea sell wool and cloth and buy wine. A merchant comes for the wine, the honey and the dyers' roots, for the orders of two rich abbeys, and for the weeks of the fair, when every toll in the district is the saint's and not the count's.
ports.seasons: The year hangs on two days: Saint Denis's, the ninth of October, when the fair opens for a month (some say until Saint Andrew's) with the new wine still working in the cask, and the day the church was hallowed, late in February, when there is a smaller fair. The river has no tide here and no bar: it runs high and brown after the thaw and low at harvest, froze hard enough for carts in the winter of 821-822, and came over its banks in 834 and 886. The grapes are cut about Michaelmas; the hungry time is from Easter to the first sheaves.

history.text: About this year King Clovis began the church of the Holy Apostles on the hill of the left bank. He lies in it, with Queen Clotilde and the holy woman Genevieve.
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Abbaye Sainte-Geneviève de Paris (dossier W:Ste-Gen)

history.text: About this year Saint Vincent's in the left-bank meadows was hallowed: a roof of gilded copper, a floor of mosaic, columns of marble. Bishop Germain's body has lain behind its high altar since 25 July 754 (or 756).
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Abbaye de Saint-Germain-des-Prés (dossier W:SGP)

history.text: The count of Paris claimed half the toll of the fair and lost before the king. The judgment says the fair had been moved 'because of a disaster' from Saint-Denis to Paris, between Saint Martin's and Saint Laurence's.
history.source: J. Tardif, Monuments historiques (1866) no. 44, 13 December 710 (dossier T 44)

history.text: The monks told King Pippin that merchants were staying away: since Charles Martel's day the count had taken four pennies a head from every free merchant, and five from a slave, who first had to swear he was one. Pippin struck the tax down and confirmed that every toll of the fair is the abbey's. Saxons (English) and Frisians are named among those who come 'to buy wine in the ports and on the rivers'.
history.source: Tardif no. 55, 8 July 753 (dossier T 55); the words quoted are the dossier's rendering of the Latin

history.text: On 24 February Abbot Fulrad's new church at Saint-Denis was hallowed before King Charles: three aisles, a ring crypt, King Pippin's grave before the west door. About this year Charles confirmed the fair's tolls to the abbey from Saint Denis's Mass until the market ends: on ships, harbours, carts and pack beasts, and the wheel, bridge and gate tolls.
history.source: archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Carolingian basilica; Tardif no. 77 (dossier SD:basilica, T 77)

history.text: On 27 March the king freed the traders of Saint-Germain from toll at Rouen, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht, Dorestad and Paris.
history.source: Tardif no. 81 (dossier T 81)

history.text: Fardulf, a Lombard priest, was given the abbey of Saint-Denis for uncovering the plot of the king's son Pippin the Hunchback the year before. Stephen has been count since 779; Erchanrad is bishop.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum, revised text, 792 (ed. Kurze 1895); fr.wikipedia, Fardulf; Liste des comtes de Paris; Liste des évêques de Paris (dossier ARF 792, W:Fardulf, W:Comtes, W:Évêques)

history.text: A description of the church of Saint-Denis gives it 245 feet, 101 windows, and doors of gold, silver and ivory. It is copied from one of Saint Martin's at Tours, with the numbers made bigger.
history.source: archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Description of the basilica in 799 (dossier SD:799)

history.text: In summer King Charles passed through Paris. It is the only time he is recorded here in the game's years.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 800 (dossier ARF 800); fr.wikipedia, Palais de la Cité

history.text: Abbot Fardulf and Count Stephen were named the king's envoys for Paris, Meaux, Melun, Provins, Étampes, Chartres and Poissy.
history.source: MGH Capitularia I (ed. Boretius 1883) no. 34 (dossier Capit 802)

history.text: Count Stephen had the new chapters of the Salic law read in the public court at Paris before the law-finders. All agreed and set their hands to them.
history.source: MGH Capitularia I, preface to the additions to Salic law (dossier Capit 803)

history.text: In the winter of 821-822 the Seine froze so hard that carts crossed on the ice.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 821; chronicle_793.json 821-winter-rivers-frozen

history.text: Greek envoys brought the emperor a book of Dionysius the Areopagite. Abbot Hilduin, who held that his own saint was that Dionysius, had it put into Latin.
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Hilduin de Saint-Denis (dossier W:Hilduin)

history.text: Hilduin built a chapel behind the church of Saint-Denis, where eight monks sang Mass day and night. In this year the Croult, a canal over six kilometres long that feeds the abbey, is first named.
history.source: archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, royal abbey; Croult (dossier SD:abbey, SD:croult)

history.text: The Seine was in flood. On 1 March, in the church of Saint-Denis, the bishops gave the emperor Louis back his arms.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 834 (ed. Waitz 1883); chronicle_793.json 834-03-01-louis-restored

history.text: After a hard winter 120 ships came up the Seine in March and reached Paris at Easter with no one resisting. The king paid 7,000 pounds of silver for them to go. The annal names no leader. The monks had carried Germain and Genevieve away.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 845; chronicle_793.json 845-03-28-paris-sacked (the day is 28 or 29 March: say 'at Easter'); fr.wikipedia, Siège de Paris (845)

history.text: On 28 December Danes took Paris and burned every church but Saint Stephen's, Saint Vincent's and Saint Denis's, which paid a great sum. The Holy Apostles on the hill burned.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 857 (dossier AB 857)

history.text: Abbot Louis of Saint-Denis and his brother Gozlin were seized by Northmen. Saint-Denis alone gave 685 pounds of gold and 3,250 of silver toward the ransom. On 21 September of the next year the martyrs' bones were carried to Nogent.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 858 and note, 859 (dossier AB 858, AB 859)

history.text: In January Paris and Saint-Germain were burned. Merchants fleeing up the river by boat were chased and caught.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 861 (dossier AB 861)

history.text: The edict of Pîtres: a new penny with the king's monogram on one side and the city's name and a cross on the other, struck at ten mints only, Paris among them; and no mail coat, weapon or horse to a Northman, on pain of death.
history.source: Edict of Pîtres, 25 June 864, chapters 11, 12, 25 (MGH Capitularia II no. 273); chronicle_793.json 864-06-25-pitres

history.text: Two hundred Northmen came to Paris for wine, found none, and went back unharmed. On 20 October Northmen entered Saint-Denis and stayed about twenty days, carrying plunder to their ships. They left their island by the abbey in June 866.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 865, 866 (dossier AB 865, AB 866)

history.text: To pay the Northmen 4,000 pounds of silver the king took a levy on every farm and a tenth of all that merchants were seen to have. Part was paid in wine.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 866 (dossier AB 866)

history.text: King Charles, who had kept the abbey for himself since Abbot Louis died on 9 January 867, had a stronghold of wood and stone built round Saint-Denis: about eight hectares, with a double ditch fed by the Croult.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 867, 869; archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, fortification (dossier AB 867, AB 869, SD:castellum)

history.text: King Charles died in the Alps on 6 October, asking to lie at Saint-Denis. His men gutted him, filled him with wine and spices, and at last put him in a pitched barrel wrapped in hides. The smell beat them; they buried him, barrel and all, at Nantua.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 877 (dossier AB 877)

history.text: On 24 November the great fleet came to Paris. Count Odo, Bishop Gozlin and Abbot Ebles held the island. On 6 February 886 a flood broke the Little Bridge and its tower was burned with the twelve men in it. Gozlin died on 16 April. In November the emperor promised 700 pounds and let the fleet winter in Burgundy.
history.source: Abbo of Saint-Germain, Bella Parisiacae urbis; fr.wikipedia, Siège de Paris (885-887); chronicle_793.json 885-11-24-siege-paris. The 700 ships and 40,000 men are Abbo's; modern guesses are 200 to 300 ships

history.text: Count Odo was made king. Saint Germain's bones were carried home to the meadows.
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Abbaye de Saint-Germain-des-Prés; Liste des comtes de Paris (dossier W:SGP, W:Comtes)

history.text: A shoemakers' shop inside the stronghold of Saint-Denis is named. Its offcuts were found in the ditch. The abbey's first mill is named in 894.
history.source: archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Carolingian shoemaker; mills (dossier SD:shoemaker, SD:mills)

history.text: In autumn the emperor Otto II camped on Montmartre, burned a suburb, and left on 30 November.
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Siège de Paris (978) (dossier W:978)

history.text: Hugh Capet, count of Paris, was made king. Bouchard of Vendôme held the county after him and died a monk in 1007: there were no more counts.
history.source: fr.wikipedia, Liste des comtes de Paris; Bouchard Ier de Vendôme (dossier W:Comtes, W:Bouchard)

history.text: On 9 June the fair called the Lendit was first held at Saint-Denis. In 1059-1060 King Henry refounded Saint Martin's on the road north.
history.source: archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Lendit fair; fr.wikipedia, Prieuré Saint-Martin-des-Champs (dossier SD:lendit, W:SMC)

eras.text: The old king's years. A Lombard abbot at Saint-Denis and an old count on the island share the district and watch each other. No king lives here. The fair is full of Frisians; the English stay away until the kings make peace in 796, and wool is dear. In 793 and 794 the abbeys feed hundreds at their gates. The new heavy penny comes in the first winter. From 804 Saxon families are said to be set down on church land up the river (?).

The abbeys' great years. Hilduin, the emperor's own chaplain, rules Saint-Denis like a lord: a Greek book, a chapel where the Mass never stops, parchment bought by the bundle. At Saint-Germain Abbot Irminon has every farm and tenant written down. The river freezes in 821-822 and floods in 834. Nobody has yet seen a Northman's ship above Rotomagus.

The fleets. In 845 the fair's silver goes into the Northmen's scales; in 856-857 and again in 861 the city burns. The saints' bones are carried away and brought back. Northmen sit on the island beside the abbey for most of a year. The fair is thin, the king takes a tenth of what merchants are seen to have, and men of the city keep a boat ready and the wine hidden.

Walls and bridges. Saint-Denis stands inside a stronghold of wood and stone with a double ditch, and the fair is held behind it. On the island the old wall is mended and the king's new Great Bridge shuts the river. In the winter of 885-886 the city holds against the great fleet for a year, and its count is made king.

The counts' city. The counts of Paris are abbots of Saint-Denis too, and greater than the king. The abbey has mills on its canal and shoemakers inside its wall. From 911 a baptised Northman holds Rotomagus and takes the toll of the lower river, which is quiet again. In 978 an emperor from the east camps on Montmartre and goes home.

The king's island. The count is king from 987 and there are no more counts. King Robert rebuilds the palace with a King's Hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas; Abbot Morard builds Saint-Germain a tower. The suburb on the right bank gets a bank and ditch. From 1053 there is a second great fair in June. Every keel from the sea passes the duke of the Normans' toll at Rotomagus.

sites.name: The strand under the island wall
sites.see: A strip of grey mud and river gravel between the water and an old stone wall twice a man's height, boats drawn up bow first and wine casks rolled on planks. Behind the wall, tiled roofs and the long ridge of the great church at the island's east end. The river is wide, slow and green-brown; it smells of wet oak, lees and cook-fires, and the carters shout in Romance.
sites.source: the 4th-century wall set 15 to 30 m back from the water, so that boats can land under it at low water (fr.wikipedia, Enceintes de Paris; Île de la Cité). Where boats really lay is not recorded: the charter of 753 says only 'ports' (Tardif no. 55)

sites.name: The Great Bridge
sites.see: A long timber bridge on piles from the island to the right bank, loud with carts and pack beasts, the water sliding dark between the posts. On the far side a round church inside a ditch and a road going north to the saint. From the 870s the bridge is the king's new one, low enough to stop a ship, with a stone tower at its bank end that is still unfinished when the great fleet comes.
sites.source: two timber bridges, north and south; Charles the Bald's new Great Bridge and its stone tower, unfinished in November 885 (fr.wikipedia, Pont au Change; Siège de Paris (885-887); Abbo). Saint-Germain-le-Rond, round and ringed by a ditch (fr.wikipedia, Église Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois). No towers before the 870s. The wheel, bridge and gate tolls are the abbey's during the fair (Tardif no. 77)

sites.name: The market between the palace and the church
sites.see: A trodden open place in the middle of the island: trestles of leeks, cheeses, salt fish and bread, wine sold by the jug from a cask on a cart, a woman with baskets of blue dye balls. At the west end the grey mass of the count's house, at the east the church roofs. Pigs, bells, and a crier giving the count's orders in two tongues.
sites.source: palace at the west end, the bishop's churches at the east, a market between (fr.wikipedia, Île de la Cité). The stalls are invented in the period's manner; woad at the Seine fairs from Design/content/economy/cloth_wool.md

sites.name: The count's house
sites.see: The old Roman citadel at the island's west end: high patched walls of small stone and red tile, a gate with spearmen, a yard where the count's court sits on benches in the open on its days. Facing the gate, the plain house of the nuns of Saint Martial. After the year 1000 the king's new hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas stand here and the walls are whole again.
sites.source: the Roman citadel, about one hectare, house of the counts; rebuilt by Robert II (996-1031) with a King's Hall and a chapel of Saint Nicholas; Saint Martial's nuns, founded 635, facing it (fr.wikipedia, Palais de la Cité). The public court and its law-finders: MGH Capitularia I, 803

sites.name: The moneyers' bench
sites.see: A low stone room by the count's gate, shuttered on the street side: a charcoal hearth, an anvil set in an oak stump, two men striking in turn, a third weighing blanks on a small balance by the one window. The pennies name the king and the city and nobody else. The ring of the hammer carries over the market.
sites.source: pennies of Pippin; of Charles before 793 (CARO/LVS, PRI/SVS, about 1.1 g); of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald (PARISII): M. Prou, Les monnaies carolingiennes (1896); Numista. One of ten mints allowed in 864 (Edict of Pîtres c. 12). Where the mint stood is not known: beside the count's house is a guess (?). No moneyer is named

sites.name: Saint Stephen's, the bishop's church
sites.see: A very long, low church of five aisles on rows of marble columns taken from older buildings, its floor and walls bright with old mosaic where the damp has spared it. Behind it a smaller church of Saint Mary, beside it the round baptistery of Saint John. Candle smoke, cold stone, and the bishop's clerks talking in the porch.
sites.source: Saint Stephen's, 70 m by 36 m, five aisles on marble columns, mosaics; Saint Mary's behind, the baptistery of Saint John beside; the council of 829 sat here; spared in 856-857 for a payment (fr.wikipedia, Cathédrale Saint-Étienne de Paris; Annales Bertiniani 857). The church that stands today was begun in 1163

sites.name: The house by the Little Bridge
sites.see: A timber house on stone footings where the southern bridge comes onto the island: one long room, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the thatch, benches, a loft with straw for lodgers, casks on trestles at the back. In October it is full of Frisian and English voices and wet cloaks. It smells of leeks, new wine and eels.
sites.source: invented: an ale-house and lodging; Frisian and Saxon (English) merchants at the fair (Tardif nos. 44, 55); the Little Bridge of timber, with a timber tower only from the 870s (Abbo)

sites.name: Saint Vincent's and Saint Germain's in the meadows
sites.see: Across the Little Bridge and west through wet meadows: a church whose roof of gilded copper shows from the river like a second sun, a wide graveyard about it, barns, a walled yard with carts of casks. Inside, marble columns, a mosaic floor, and lamps before the saint's tomb behind the high altar. After 861 the roof is black timber for a generation; from about the year 1000 a new stone tower stands at the west door.
sites.source: hallowed about 558; gilded copper roof, mosaic floor, marble columns; Germain's body behind the high altar since 754 (or 756); a large graveyard; burned in 861; rebuilt by Abbot Morard (990-1014), whose tower stands (fr.wikipedia, Abbaye de Saint-Germain-des-Prés). Abbot Irminon's book of estates, about 823-828 (fr.wikipedia, Polyptyque d'Irminon)

sites.name: The saint's landing
sites.see: A low bank on the outside of a great bend, a day's rowing below the city by water and two hours from it by road: posts, a plank stage, a toll man's table under a hide awning, carts waiting to go up to the abbey, whose roof stands over the fields to the east. A long wooded island lies in the stream opposite. In the fair's weeks boats lie three deep and the mud is ankle deep.
sites.source: coming up from Rouen a skipper reaches Saint-Denis first, for the river loops north below the city; an island lies in the river beside the abbey, the Northmen's in 865-866 (fr.wikipedia, Seine; Annales Bertiniani 866). The tolls on ships and harbours are the abbey's (Tardif nos. 55, 77). The stage and table are invented

sites.name: Saint Denis's church
sites.see: A tall stone church of three aisles, new in the old king's day, with a bronze-bound west door and a king's grave slab set in the ground before it. Inside, many small windows, a raised choir, and steps down to a ring passage where the three martyrs lie. North of it a two-storey stone hall for great guests, and beyond that a graveyard as wide as a field. From 869 all of it stands inside a bank, a timber wall and two wet ditches.
sites.source: Fulrad's church, hallowed 24 February 775: three aisles, a ring crypt, Pippin's grave before the west door; Hilduin's chapel of 832; a stone hall north of the church, two storeys, at least 30 m by 14 m; the great graveyard, over 8,000 square metres; the stronghold of 869 (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis: basilica, royal abbey, fortification; Annales Bertiniani 869). The kings buried here: Dagobert, Charles Martel (741), Pippin (768)

sites.name: The hospice at the abbey gate
sites.see: A long low house against the abbey's outer gate, with a porch where a monk stands at a half-door handing out loaves and bowls. In front, people sitting on the ground in rows: old men, women with children, a pilgrim with a staff. Behind, the smoke of the bakehouse and the sound of water running in a stone channel. It smells of barley bread and too many people.
sites.source: the monastery's bakery, kitchen and baths, and a hospice at the gate; an aqueduct that fed three stone tanks (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, royal abbey; aqueduct). The crowd of 793-794 is the spine's thread hungry_years: the numbers fed are not recorded (?)

sites.name: The fair of Saint Denis
sites.see: Rows of booths of poles, hides and wattle on open ground by the abbey: bolts of grey and blue cloth on trestles, sacks of wool, crocks of honey, baskets of red root and blue dye balls, and everywhere casks, with a monk chalking them. Englishmen and Frisians shouting prices in their own tongues, a Greek word from a spice seller, the abbey's bell over all. In later years the booths stand among the graves, at two pennies a pitch, and from 869 inside the wall.
sites.source: the fair from Saint Denis's day, 9 October (Tardif no. 77; fairs_793.json: 28 days); wine out, wool and woollen cloth in, the abbey's grain, spare wine and honey sold (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Saint-Denis fair). Later the stalls stood in the graveyard at two pennies a pitch. Where the fair stood in 793 is not known: the judgment of 710 has it moved to Paris, the charters of 753 and 775 speak of the market and the city both. Madder at the fair is from a forged charter (?)

people.name: Fardulf
people.trait: A Lombard priest who came north in a beaten king's following and rose by telling King Charles of his own son's plot: learned, watchful, grateful, and never quite at home.
people.want: The abbey rich, its fair full and its tolls whole; verses that outlast him; to be thought loyal and not merely useful.
people.fear: The word 'informer' said where he can hear it; a count's hand in the saint's tolls.
people.voice: Soft and careful, with a southern turn to his Romance; praises the king in every third sentence and means it.
people.looks: About fifty-five, lean, dark-eyed, olive-skinned, a grey tonsure, a black wool habit of good cloth, a plain abbot's staff and a small wax tablet in his sleeve.
knows: the judgments of 710 and 753 and the charter of 775 on the fair's tolls, nearly word for word
what the abbey's cellar holds and what it will sell this fair
what was said at court a season ago, and who is in favour
the plot of 792, of which he will not speak
what parchment, pigment and wax cost, and who brings them

ties.note: The king's fellow envoys in 802, and each other's oldest quarrel: the abbey holds the fair's tolls that the count's office has claimed since 710.
His cellarer loses every note he writes and has never lost a cask. The abbot has stopped asking for the notes.
Trusts his lay toll man's count over his own monks' and says so, which the monks remember.
Two foreigners who wrote verse at the same court; a letter passes now and then (invented in detail) (?).
The abbot who takes the king's tolls on the coast sees every ship before the saint's fair does.
Writes to the wic-reeve about ground at Lundenwic that the saint claims; the charter for it is a doubtful one (?).
Sends word down the river each September of what the fair lacks.
The chief singer of Rouen has had a psalter of the abbey's for nine years. Fardulf asks after it by every boat.
her house inside Rouen's river gate pays the saint a rent in ale (?); he has never tasted it and asks after it by every boat
sells Saint-Wandrille's schoolmaster the fair's second-best skins at the abbey's price, and admires the hand they come back in
Saint Germain's cellarer sells without a fair and passes without a toll; the abbot pretends not to mind

lines.greet: You are welcome to the saint's house. The fair is his, the tolls are his, and the peace is the king's. What do you carry?
lines.greet_again: The shipman again. The saint remembers those who come back. So does my cellarer, who writes it down.
lines.greet_friend: Come in out of the dust. I have a verse to try on someone who will not flatter me. You are the nearest I have.
rumour: The king's son plotted against him and is shorn a monk now. I say no more. I have said enough about that already.
The English stay away again this year. Their king and ours are not speaking. Wool is dear, and you are not English.
At the gate we feed more each day. They tell of grain that stood in the ear and was dust in the hand.
lines.saying: I served a king who lost, then a king who won. The second is easier on the knees.
lines.farewell: Go with God and Saint Denis. Come at the feast, not after it. After it the wine is sold, and so is the news.

people.source: Fardulf, a Lombard, abbot of Saint-Denis 793-806, given the abbey for uncovering the plot of Pippin the Hunchback (Annales regni Francorum, revised text, 792; fr.wikipedia, Fardulf); envoy with Count Stephen in 802 (MGH Capit. I no. 34). His birth year, his verses in conversation and his temper are invented (?). 'romance' stands for a Lombard: the game has no Lombard people

people.name: Stephen
people.trait: Count of Paris since before most of his men were grown: a soldier turned judge, who knows the Salic law by its fines and grudges every penny that goes north to the monks.
people.want: His court obeyed and the law read and signed; a share of the fair, which three kings have refused his office.
people.fear: The king's envoys asking how tolls are taken in his district. He is one of them, and knows what they ask.
people.voice: Blunt Frankish and blunter Romance, short orders, counts in shillings; laughs once, and late.
people.looks: Near sixty, thick-necked, a long grey moustache and a shaved chin, a blue cloak pinned at the right shoulder, a sword with a worn grip, a heavy ring.
knows: the Salic law by its fines, and the new chapters read in his court
who has a suit before the law-finders and who will lose it
the old head-penny of the fair: four for a free man, five for a slave
the roads and landings to Meaux, Melun, Chartres and Poissy
when the king's envoys ride, being one

ties.note: Rides beside him as the king's envoy and counts the abbey's carts on the way.
Sends a man to stand by the toll table and count heads, to no lawful purpose.
Counts who meet at the king's assemblies and agree that merchants are getting above themselves (invented).
An abbot holds the king's tolls on the coast that a count might have had.
The count of the Breton march, from 799: they meet at the king's assemblies and trade complaints about bishops (invented).

lines.greet: A stranger with a boat. In my district you answer to my court for blood and theft. For tolls, this month, ask the monks.
lines.greet_again: You. No complaint has been brought against you since last time. That is how I like to know a merchant.
lines.greet_friend: Sit on my bench. You have brought the hounds you promised, or the news. Either will do.
rumour: My grandfather's count took four pennies a head at the fair. King Pippin stopped it. The monks have not stopped telling me.
The new chapters of the law were read in my court. Every law-finder set his hand to them. Now no man can say he did not hear.
The king came through in summer. He looked at the bridges and not at me. That is the best a count can hope for.
lines.saying: A free man swore and paid four. A slave swore and paid five. Honesty has always cost a little extra.
lines.farewell: Go. Keep your men off the bridge after dark, and your knives sheathed on market days.

people.source: Stephen, count of Paris 779 to 811 or 815 (fr.wikipedia, Liste des comtes de Paris); envoy in 802; had the additions to Salic law read in the public court in 803 (MGH Capit. I). The head-penny: Tardif no. 55. His birth year, looks and grudge are invented (?); the year of his death is not sure

people.name: Dominicus
people.trait: The abbey's lay toll man at the landing and the fair: a vine-dresser's son who reckons faster than the monks who check him, and enjoys it.
people.want: Every keel, cart and pack beast counted; a merchant who says what he has before he is asked.
people.fear: The count's agents setting up a table beside his own; the cellarer's recount.
people.voice: Quick Romance, counts aloud on his fingers, and gives your answer back to you as a question.
people.looks: About forty, small and wiry, sunburnt, black hair cut round, a short brown tunic belted high, a notched tally stick as long as his arm and a lead token of the abbey on a thong.
knows: the toll on a ship, a cart, a pack beast, a wheel, the bridge and the gate
who has come to the fair this year and what each declared
which merchants pass free on an abbey's letter, and whether the letter is good
what this year's wine is worth before the cellarer has said
the loops of the river down to Rotomagus and how many days each costs

ties.note: Takes the saint's tolls for the abbot and answers to him alone.
The count's man stands by his table every October. Dominicus counts him too.
His mother's sister. He eats at her house and hears there what the Frisians did not declare.
The cellarer recounts everything the toll man has counted, and comes out one cask different.
Must let Saint Germain's traders pass free by the charter of 779, and reads the letter through every year in hope.
They send word up and down the river of who is coming and what he swore to.
Thiadbod once declared forty bolts as thirty. Dominicus counted them on the bank, aloud.
Has never met him; they know each other by the merchants who complain of both.

lines.greet: From the sea? Then you saw the saint's roof before the city's. Good. How many keels, how many heads, and what is in the hold?
lines.greet_again: Four heads and cloth, last year. Four heads and cloth again? Say it yourself. I like to hear it agree.
lines.greet_friend: Tie up at the near post, it is the dry one. I told the cellarer you were coming. He pretended not to care.
rumour: The count's man stood by my table yesterday, counting heads. I counted him. One head. He owes the saint a penny.
Saint Germain's men pass free on their abbot's letter. I read it every year. It has not changed. I keep hoping.
The English are back with their cloaks. The king wrote that they must be the old length. I have a stick for that.
lines.saying: A merchant's memory is short. That is why the stick is long.
lines.to_heir: Your father said 'four heads' before I could ask. You stood beside him, so high. Now you say it.
lines.farewell: Go down with the stream. At Rotomagus say Dominicus counted you. It saves them the trouble of believing you.

people.source: invented; the abbey's toll men and the count's agents are in the charters (Tardif nos. 55, 77), none by name. The name is a Romance one of the time (names_placeholder.json); the monk Natalis at Herio is another man. The cloaks' length: Charles's letter to Offa, 796 (the spine's thread black_stones)

people.name: Waldric
people.trait: Cellarer of Saint Denis's: holds that every cask on the Seine is the saint's until proved otherwise, and writes everything down on strips of parchment that he then cannot find.
people.want: The cellar emptied at the fair at a good price and filled again by Martinmas; skins for the writing room; a carrier he need not count after.
people.fear: A sour vintage sold under the abbey's mark; the toll man's count differing from his own in front of the abbot.
people.voice: Brisk Romance with a Frankish edge, taps each cask as he names it, and does his sums aloud.
people.looks: About forty-five, round-shouldered and quick, tonsured, chalk on both sleeves of his habit, a lump of chalk, a tasting cup and strips of parchment stuck in his belt.
knows: the three rows of the long storehouse: this year's wine, last year's, and the abbot's own
how many the gate fed yesterday and what is left in the barn
what a bundle of parchment is worth and which seller's leaves have holes
who pays the abbey late, being one who pays others late
how new wine behaves in a boat in the first frost

ties.note: Answers to the abbot for every cask, loaf and skin.
Counts again whatever the toll man has counted.
Saint Germain's cellarer sells quietly what Waldric sells aloud, and looks down on him for it.
The cooper of Rouen hoops and tops the abbey's casks on their way down, and is paid at the next fair, late.
Tells the king's toll man at the river gate that every cask is the saint's own and so goes free.
Sells Saint-Wandrille's school the parchment his own scribes pass over, at the abbey's price.
Has never met the count's steward at Dorestad, but his wine is on that table and his reckoning with it (invented).
Saint-Wandrille's cellarer will not agree that every cask on the river is Saint Denis's, having a saint of his own

lines.greet: A boat, and room in it. Good. Three rows: this year's, last year's, and the abbot's own. Which can you afford to be wrong about?
lines.greet_again: I wrote your name on a strip and put it somewhere safe. No matter, I know the face. The same casks?
lines.greet_friend: Come through. I kept back four of last year's for you and told the abbot they had leaked. Do not thank me aloud.
rumour: We baked for three hundred at the gate yesterday. I am a cellarer, not a miracle. Bring rye and I will pay in wine.
The scribes want calfskin without holes. A hundred leaves, sixty pennies. They hold each one to the light, like a woman with an egg.
The toll man at Rouen wants a penny on casks that are plainly the saint's. I have written to the abbot. Twice.
lines.saying: New wine and a new friend: do not drive the bung home on either too soon.
lines.farewell: Go with the stream. Ease the bungs if it works, fill them up if it sinks, and bring my casks back empty, not broken.

people.source: invented: Brother Waldric the cellarer is the wine fleet chain's man (encounters/chain_wine_fleet_793.json, cards s04 and after) and the neighbouring ports' parisius.waldric. The abbey sold its grain and spare wine (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Saint-Denis fair); the saying turns Ecclesiasticus 9:10, 'a new friend is as new wine'

people.name: Ermentrud
people.trait: A boatman's widow who has lodged the Frisians every October since she could see over the table: forgets no face, no debt and no kindness.
people.want: Her benches full at the fair, her vines on the hill dressed by someone who knows how, and word in winter of the men who slept in her loft.
people.fear: A dry cask in October; the river in her cellar; a lodger dying under her roof far from his kin.
people.voice: Warm, fast and scolding; calls grown shipmasters 'boy' and tells them what they ate last time.
people.looks: About fifty, broad, red-handed, a linen head-cloth tied behind, a dark wool gown kilted up for work, a ring of keys and a wooden cup on a cord at her waist.
knows: who is in the city, in whose house, and for how long
which grower's wine on the left-bank hill is sound this year
what the Frisians and the English said at her table
where to hire a man who knows the river's bends
how to nurse the autumn fever, and when not to move a man

ties.note: Her sister's son. She feeds him and he tells her nothing, which she gets round.
Holds her strip of vines of Saint Germain's and pays the abbey in wine each Martinmas.
He has lodged with her twenty Octobers and paid for nineteen; she holds one of his cloaks against the twentieth.
Two ale-wives who have never met and send each other greetings, and warnings, by the same shipmen.
Buys her casks from him and sends him every lodger whose hoops are slack.
Wiltrud's salt comes up to her each autumn with a message scratched on the sack stick.
The ale-wife inside Rouen's river gate: each sends the other her lodgers, with a word on which ones pay.
her daughter's grandson, born after her time, who keeps her bench for Frisians in a house twice rebuilt

lines.greet: A new face off a Frisian boat. Sit, boy. Bread first, then tell me whose son you are and who sent you.
lines.greet_again: You had the eel and left the leeks. Same bench. Your steersman owes me for a cup. Tell him I said so.
lines.greet_friend: There you are. I kept the dry corner and turned two Englishmen away for it. Do not make me regret them.
rumour: The new wine is thin this year, but honest. The abbey will sell last year's dear. Buy on the hill, from the growers.
A Frisian took the fever at the fair and lay in my loft till Martinmas. His partner sailed with both their casks.
The monks at the gate cannot bake fast enough. People walk in from the south country with nothing. I send my crusts.
lines.saying: The river brings every man twice: once to sell, and once to say what went wrong.
lines.to_heir: You have your father's ears. He sat there and lied to me about the weather at sea. Sit.
lines.farewell: Go on, then. Keep your feet dry and come back in October. I count my lodgers like my hens.

people.source: invented; Frisian and English merchants at the fair (Tardif nos. 44, 55); tenants who owe wine to Saint-Germain are the matter of Irminon's book of estates (fr.wikipedia, Polyptyque d'Irminon). The name is built from attested Frankish parts (Ermen- + -trud), as borne by tenants in Romance-speaking Neustria

people.name: Frotbald
people.trait: Cellarer of Saint Germain's: keeper of the abbey's wine, its traders and its toll letter, who thinks the monks of Saint Denis are stallholders in habits.
people.want: Cloth for the brothers' backs without paying the fair's price; wax for the altars; a carrier who loses nothing.
people.fear: The abbot's book of estates, in which every cask he ever mislaid will have a line.
people.voice: Dry and slow, lists things in threes, and never names a price first.
people.looks: Mid-forties, tall and stooped, tonsured, a habit patched at the elbows and in winter a sheepskin pelisse to the heels and mittens, a ring of keys and a small tasting cup.
knows: the charter of 779: Saint Germain's traders free of toll at Rouen, Quentovic, Amiens, Maastricht, Dorestad and Paris
what each of the abbey's estates sends in wine, and when the carts come
who Saint Germain's own traders are and where they are this season
what cloth is worth by its length and its dye
which of his neighbour's monks is selling what at the gate

ties.note: Shows him the same letter every year and watches him read it.
The other abbey has the fair. Saint Germain's has the older saint, he says, and the better roof.
Two cellarers on one river. Each is sure the other waters the wine he sells.
Her wine is the best that comes in as rent, and he tells nobody.
His traders show the charter at Dorestad every summer; the toll man there has tried to out-read it.
The abbot's clerks at Quentovic honour the letter without being asked twice.
Saint Germain's own man at the wic: Frotbald sends him wine and orders, and no leave to come home.

lines.greet: A Frisian with cloth. The saint's own traders go free at Dorestat, Quentovic and Rouen. You do not. Let us talk about that.
lines.greet_again: You lost nothing last time. Not a bolt, not a cake of wax. I wrote it down, which is the same as praise.
lines.greet_friend: Come into the cool. Three things: the abbot is counting, the wine is good, and I have an errand that only you get.
rumour: The abbot is having every farm, hen and man written in a book. He began with my cellar. I have slept badly since.
Saxon families were set down on church land up the river, they say, by the king's order. They speak to nobody.
Saint Denis's monks sell at their gate like stallholders. We sell too. But we do not enjoy it so openly.
lines.saying: Wine is for the altar and the lord. What is left over is for sale. There is always something left over.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Bring it all back, or bring the reason in writing. I prefer it all.

people.source: invented (the name from attested parts, Frot- + -bald); the id parisius.cellarer is the one the neighbouring ports use for Saint-Germain's cellarer; Saint-Germain's own traders and their freedom from toll, 27 March 779 (Tardif no. 81); Abbot Irminon's book of estates, about 823-828; the monk's pelisse and mittens by the rule of 816-817 (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Carolingian shoemaker). The Saxon families by Parisius in 804-815 are the spine's (thread saxon_end): the dossier found no source for them (?)

people.name: Hilduin
people.trait: Abbot of Saint-Denis and a great man at the emperor's court: restless, splendid, and sure that his saint is the Athenian who heard the apostle Paul.
people.want: His saint's fame: the Greek book in Latin, a Passion worthy of the name, a chapel where the Mass never stops, and skins enough to write it all on.
people.fear: Backing the wrong side in the emperor's house; a plain man asking how he knows who his saint was.
people.voice: Quick and courtly; speaks of the saint as of a living patron with the emperor's ear, and asks what the Greeks would pay for a thing.
people.looks: About forty, tall, well fed, a fine dark habit under a fur-lined cloak, a gold ring, a jewelled book held shut under one arm.
knows: the Greek book the envoys brought in 827 and how the work of turning it goes
the mind of the court, a season ahead of the river
what calfskin, gold leaf and blue pigment cost, and who has them
which churches would give silver for a copy of his Passion of the saint
what the Greeks' envoys ate, wore and bought

ties.note: Hears the northern mission's news at court and sends the monk of Corbie parchment for his books (invented in detail) (?).
Followed the old archbishop of Cologne as the emperor's chaplain (?) and learned the court from him.
The emperor's man, most years.
A palace clerk who copies for him and is paid in letters.
The abbot of the island house in the bay sends him its book of the saint's miracles and looks to him at court.
The young monk who writes the miracles of Saint Philibert sends him the first book about 838-840, to be corrected.

lines.greet: You stand in the house of the Areopagite, shipman, who heard the apostle at Athens. What have you brought him?
lines.greet_again: The one who brought the skins dry. Good. A wet skin is a psalm lost.
lines.greet_friend: Walk with me. Eight brothers sing in the new chapel day and night. You can tell me your prices between the psalms.
rumour: The Greek emperor sent our lord a book of the saint's own writing. I am having it put into Latin. It is not easy Greek.
The river froze so hard that carts crossed it for a month. The fair's wine went home by sledge. Some of it arrived.
They gave the emperor back his sword-belt in this church, with the river over its banks. I was elsewhere that day.
lines.saying: A saint without a book is a rumour. I am writing the book.
lines.farewell: Go, and come at the feast with calfskin. Thick for the Gospels, thin for letters, and none of it goat.

people.source: Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis 814-841 (fr.wikipedia, Liste des abbés de Saint-Denis; Hilduin de Saint-Denis): the Greek book of 827 put into Latin; the chapel of 832; his Passion of Saint Denis, 835-840, the first to say the saint carried his head. That he was the emperor's archchaplain after Hildebold of Cologne, and sided against the emperor in 830, is from memory (?). His birth year and death year are not sure; his words are invented

people.name: Hildegaud
people.trait: A wine merchant of the island with his own boat, who was chased up the river by the Danes as a young man and has reckoned every year since as profit.
people.want: A partner with a sea keel and steady nerves; his casks out before each fleet comes and his silver out of sight before each levy.
people.fear: The king's tenth, taken on all that a merchant is seen to have; the sound of many oars behind him above the city.
people.voice: Low and wry, shrugs with his whole body, and puts a price on everything, bad news included.
people.looks: Bald early, lean, a burn scar down the left forearm, a patched green cloak, a boat-hook for a walking stick and a purse worn inside his shirt.
knows: where the Northmen's ships lie this season, and whether they are buying
the landing places up the river toward Melun, and which are too shallow for a chase
the new penny of 864 and which ten mints may strike it
who paid what toward each ransom, and who was seen to have little
what the law of 864 forbids selling to a Northman: mail, weapons and horses, not wine

ties.note: Her daughter's grandson. The house by the Little Bridge is his, twice rebuilt, and the bench is still kept for Frisians.
Tells the young monk what the river looked like from the water; the monk puts none of it in.
Sends wine down to the Dane who takes the toll at Dorestad, who pays in good silver and asks no blessing.
Once passed Dorestad under Rorik's peace without paying; has been meaning to settle it.
The clerk of Rouen who keeps a list of what was burned sends a boy on a horse when sails are seen at the river mouth.
Carried grain in for the count's brother during the siege and was never paid; the debt runs the other way, he says.
bought wine of him before Bordeaux burned, and buys of his sons at the Loire after (?)
tells the monk what the river looked like from a boat with Danes behind it; the monk writes down the day

lines.greet: A sea keel at Paris. Either you are brave or nobody down the river told you. Sit. Which is it?
lines.greet_again: Still afloat, both of us. I count that a good year. What are they paying for wine where you come from?
lines.greet_friend: My grandmother's mother kept this bench for Frisians. I keep it for you. Drink, then I will tell you where the ships lie.
rumour: I was on the river the winter they burned the city. We rowed for Melun. They rowed faster. I swam.
Two hundred of them came for wine and found none. We had hidden it. They went home sober and hurt nobody. A miracle.
The king took a tenth of all a merchant was seen to have. I was seen to have very little.
Ten mints now, and this is one. The new penny has the king's name in a knot. After Martinmas the old ones are only metal.
lines.saying: Sell to the abbey before the fleet comes, and be gone before the king pays. After that nobody has a penny.
lines.farewell: Go by daylight and look behind you at the bends. If you see many oars, you never knew me.

people.source: invented; the city's merchants with their own boats, chased up the river and caught in January 861 (Annales Bertiniani 861); the two hundred who found no wine (865); the tenth of 866; the penny and the ten mints of the edict of Pîtres, 864. The name is built from attested Frankish parts (Hild- + -gaud), as borne in Romance-speaking Neustria

people.name: Abbo
people.trait: A young monk of Saint Germain's who watched the great siege from the wall and is putting it into hard Latin verse that nobody asked him for.
people.want: Witnesses: who stood where, and what was said; rare words; anyone who will hear book one to the end.
people.fear: That the city's stand will be forgotten, or told by someone who was not there.
people.voice: Eager, exact about days and names, uses a strange learned word and explains it at once; hard on Franks who love fine clothes.
people.looks: Late twenties in the siege year, thin, tonsured, ink to the knuckles, a patched black habit with soot on one sleeve, a wax tablet always in his hand.
knows: the names of the twelve who held the tower of the Little Bridge
the day the flood broke the bridge, and what was done with the hawks
that Sigfred took sixty pounds of silver and left, and the rest stayed
where Saint Germain's body was carried on the walls
the Northmen's engines: the rams, the roofed carts, the fire ships

ties.note: The old merchant is the only layman who lets him finish a line.
Put the count in his poem, at his brother's side on the wall. The count has not read it.
Holds that the lord of Rouen was among those he watched from the wall, and will not sit at a table with him (?).
The old clerk of Rouen compared dates with Abbo's master Aimoin; Abbo has the letters now and still writes to him.
his master in the cloister, who taught him to ask which year before anything else

lines.greet: A merchant, and from the north. Were you on the river in the year of the siege? No? Then sit, and I will tell you.
lines.greet_again: You came back for book two. Nobody comes back for book two. God reward you.
lines.greet_friend: Friend, listen. I have found the word for the tower's fall. It took me a month, and it is only four syllables.
rumour: Twelve men held the tower when the bridge went. I have all twelve names. Ermenfred, Eriveus, Eriland... you are not writing this down.
Before the fire reached them they let their hawks fly, so the birds should not burn. I put that in. It is true.
Sigfred took sixty pounds and went. The others stayed. A Dane keeps his word one Dane at a time.
They had one flask to throw water on the fire, and it slipped from their hands. I put that in too.
lines.saying: The Franks will lose the realm for a purple cloak and a gold pin. I wrote that as well. They liked it least.
lines.farewell: Go with Saint Germain. If you meet a man who was there, ask him where he stood, and send him to me.

people.source: Abbo of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, about 850 to after 923, author of the Bella Parisiacae urbis (fr.wikipedia, Abbon de Saint-Germain-des-Prés; the Latin at remacle.org): the twelve of the tower, the hawks, the flask, Sigfred's sixty pounds, the rebuke of the Franks' fine dress. His words here are invented. That Rollo was at the siege is Dudo's story, written about 1015 (LATER) (?)

people.name: Robert
people.trait: Count of Paris and lay abbot of Saint Denis's, brother of the count who was made king: he fought on the wall as a young man and has been making terms ever since.
people.want: The river open and paying; the Northmen at Rotomagus kept as neighbours, since they cannot be made to leave.
people.fear: A second fleet coming up past a Rotomagus that looks the other way; a king who remembers whose brother wore the crown.
people.voice: Even and unhurried, a soldier's Romance; asks a question and waits longer than is comfortable.
people.looks: In his forties, broad, a cropped greying beard, a mail shirt worn as other men wear a tunic, a red cloak, an abbot's ring on a soldier's hand.
knows: what toll is taken at Rotomagus, and by whom
who holds each bridge and each walled abbey on the Seine
what Saint Denis's fair is worth, being its abbot
where each man stood in the siege, his brother and the bishop among them
which of the king's men would rather he were king

ties.note: Said to have stood godfather at Rollo's baptism and given him his own name (Dudo of Saint-Quentin, about 1015, LATER) (?).
The same man, in his own city: they send each other envoys, hawks and warnings.
The monk who wrote the siege. Robert likes him and avoids the poem.
The old wine merchant carried grain in during the siege and has not let the count's house forget it.
the count on the Garonne sends word north whenever sails leave his river (?)

lines.greet: A merchant from the sea, and you came past Rouen with your cargo whole. Tell me what they took from you there. Exactly.
lines.greet_again: You again. Good. A man who comes twice up that river is either honest or protected. Which?
lines.greet_friend: Sit. You see Rouen more often than my envoys do, and you count better. What is he building?
rumour: The Northman at Rouen is baptised and holds the river mouth from the king. He hangs thieves. I have had worse neighbours with older crosses.
I am abbot of Saint Denis, God forgive us both. The monks pray and I keep the wall. Each thinks the other has the easy part.
My brother went out through their lines to fetch the emperor. The emperor came, and paid them. We do not speak of emperors here.
lines.saying: A wall is a promise made in timber. It wants renewing as often.
lines.farewell: Go. Pay his toll at Rouen and remember the sum. I shall ask.

people.source: Robert, count of Paris 888-922, brother of Odo, in the siege of 885-886 (Abbo; fr.wikipedia, Liste des comtes de Paris); the Robertian counts held the abbey of Saint-Denis after Ebles (fr.wikipedia, Liste des abbés de Saint-Denis). He was made king in June 922 and killed in battle at Soissons on 15 June 923 (Flodoard, Annales 922-923); his birth year is a guess (?). The godfather story is Dudo's (LATER). His words are invented

people.name: Aimoin
people.trait: A monk of Saint Germain's who writes down what the Northmen did to his house and what the saint did to them: orderly, sharp about dates, and still angry about one Easter.
people.want: The day and the year of each fleet, from someone who saw it; the names of the martyrs' bones brought up from Spain spelled as the Spaniards spell them.
people.fear: A wonder written down wrong and believed for ever after.
people.voice: Level and exact; says 'in the year' before most sentences and will stop you to ask which year.
people.looks: A grey, upright monk with a clean habit and a ruled wax tablet, a penknife on a cord, and a way of looking at a man as at a doubtful reading.
knows: the Easter of 845, when the fleet came to the city and the king paid
where the body of Saint Germain was carried each time, and when it came home
the journey of two brothers to Cordoba in 858 and what they brought back
which dates in other men's annals do not agree with his

ties.note: The young monk who will write the great siege learned his letters and his exactness from him.
The clerk of Rouen keeps a list of the taken; Aimoin keeps a list of the days. They compare (?).
The wine merchant tells him what the river looked like from a boat; Aimoin writes down the day and leaves out the fear.
A warden of Saint Wandrille's body, met on the saints' roads: they trade wonders (?).

lines.greet: You came up the river. Then you passed Rotomagus. In what state was it, and on what day? No, the day first.
lines.greet_again: The shipman who knew what day it was. Sit. I have three dates from the Loire and I believe none of them.
rumour: In the year of the first fleet they came at Easter, and the king weighed out seven thousand pounds. The saint struck them with a flux on the way home. I have the names of men who saw it.
Two of our brothers walked to Cordoba and came back with three martyrs. The Saracens' king let them go. Write that down wherever you write things.
lines.saying: A wonder without a date is a rumour in a cowl.
lines.farewell: If you see the clerk at Rotomagus, tell him the fleet he doubts was in the autumn, not the spring. He will know which.

people.source: Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Pres, who wrote the Miracles of Saint Germain (the fleet of 845 and the flights of the saint's body) and the bringing of the martyrs George, Aurelius and Nathalia from Cordoba in 858; Abbo of Saint-Germain names him as his master. Not in the dossier, but checked: a monk of the house from before 845, its archivist and chief copyist from 872, teacher of Abbo, died 9 June 889 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimoin_of_Saint-Germain-des-Prés, after A. Molinier 1901). His birth year is not known. The Rotomagus file's Einold names him: this is that man.

stories.title: Bread at the gate
stories.summary: In the hungry years the abbeys by Parisius feed hundreds at their gates, and a boat with grain can sell it dear in the market or at the king's price to the monks. The abbey remembers which, for longer than the merchant lives.
stories.picture: The half-door of a monastery hospice at dawn: a monk handing out loaves over it, rows of thin people sitting on the ground, and a merchant standing at the back with a sack on his shoulder.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year < 795
beats.text: Brother Waldric says they baked for three hundred yesterday and it was not enough. A man in the row tells of the false grain: ears that stood in the field at harvest and came to dust in the hand.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year < 795 and not flag.hy_fed_poor and not flag.hy_sold_dear
beats.text: Abbot Fardulf will take any wheat, rye or barley you can bring, at the abbey's price, which is low. In the island market the same sack fetches three times as much, and the count's men are watching who asks it.

beats.when: year < 795
beats.text: Down the river the archbishop's steward will sell seed corn from a full barn, dear, to a man who asks no questions about why the barn is full.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 794 and year < 797
beats.text: The king's ruling from Frankfurt is cried at the fair: a measure of oats one penny, barley two, rye three, wheat four, and one new measure for the whole realm. Dominicus sets your measure beside the abbey's new one and looks at you.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 805 and year < 808
beats.text: Hunger again, and a law against carrying food out of the realm. The porter is a new man, but the old one left a list. He looks for your house's name on it.

beats.when: year < 795
beats.text: The cell on the Canche feeds whoever waits on the wind, and this year the poor of the country besides. Osmund has heard what Saint-Denis bakes in a day and says he does it with one oven.

beats.when: year < 795
beats.text: A table at Saint Peter's gate outside the wall, and a row before it by first light. The brother who ladles says the abbeys up the river are feeding hundreds, and asks what rye costs where you have been.

beats.when: year < 796
beats.text: On the salt island the cellarer counts his sacks aloud. The hunger runs there too, he says, but no king's man has ever come to see what a sack fetches.

endings.how: You sold or gave grain to the abbey at its price in 793 or 794.
endings.text: The abbot has your name written where the monks pray for benefactors. In the next hunger the man at the gate knows your house, and at the fair your pitch is by the gate.
endings.reward: flag hy_fed_poor; deed and standing with the church here; the booth at the fair (parisius.work.fair_booth) is granted without the asking gift; Fardulf's feeling rises

endings.how: You sold in the island market above the king's price.
endings.text: It is the best week's silver of your year. The count's man was counting, and the count remembers a merchant who made him look slack before the king's envoys.
endings.reward: about three times the grain's worth in silver; flag hy_sold_dear: the count's court may ask about it, and the monks at the gate do not know you

endings.how: You brought no grain, but had your measure checked against the new one.
endings.text: Dominicus burns the abbey's mark into your measure. Nobody in the district can say you sell short, and you can say it of others.
endings.reward: flag hy_new_measure; haggling over grain here goes your way; Dominicus's feeling rises

stories.reward: The abbey's lasting goodwill and a place at its fair, or a quick profit and the count's eye on you.

stories.title: Skins for the saint
stories.summary: Saint-Denis buys parchment by the bundle at the October fair and never has enough. A merchant who brings it dry, year after year, is given a standing order, and under Abbot Hilduin something dearer to carry: gatherings of the saint's own book.
stories.picture: A monk at a fair booth holding a sheet of parchment up against the low October sun to look through it, a bundle of a hundred more on the trestle, a merchant waiting with wet hair.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and month = 10 and year < 842
beats.text: Brother Waldric, or the cellarer after him, goes from booth to booth buying parchment by the bundle. He holds each leaf to the light, counts a hundred, and pays sixty pennies without bargaining for the bundles that have no holes.

beats.when: year < 842
beats.text: At Saint-Wandrille's landing the master of the new school buys what parchment the fair has left and wants blue pigment. For an hour's talk he will tell you what a book is worth, and to whom. (Sets bk_knows_worth.)

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year < 842 and hold.parchment > 0
beats.text: Bring bundles to the abbey itself, twice, dry: the abbot offers a standing order. Ten bundles each fair at a fixed price, and pigments and wax tablets when you can find them. (Sets bk_parchment.)

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 827 and year < 841 and flag.bk_parchment
beats.text: Abbot Hilduin has the Greek book in Latin at last, in loose gatherings. He wants a copy carried to the court, which keeps Lent at Noviomagus, in a boat that has never wet his skins. It is worth more than the boat.

beats.when: flag.parisius_greek_book and year >= 827 and year < 842
beats.text: The palace clerk unwraps the gatherings, counts them, and reads the first line aloud twice. He signs for them. (Sets bk_carried.)

beats.when: year >= 796 and year < 827
beats.text: On the Loire the monks of Tours buy calfskin by the hundred and pay in thanks. Eadhelm says Saint-Denis may have the fair: Saint Martin's has the calves.

beats.when: year >= 830 and year < 837
beats.text: The young monk who writes the saint's wonders means to send the first book to Abbot Hilduin, to be corrected. He asks whether the abbot is as great a man as they say, and whether he is kind to scribes.

endings.how: You brought dry parchment to the abbey at two fairs.
endings.text: Your name is on the cellarer's list of those who are paid without counting. The order comes each October whether the fair is good or not.
endings.reward: flag bk_parchment: a commission for ten bundles of parchment each fair, paid on delivery at 72 d the bundle; act:read_text and act:copy_text are open to you at Saint-Denis

endings.how: You carried Hilduin's gatherings to the court and they arrived dry and whole.
endings.text: Hilduin has the house's name written in the abbey's book of the living and the dead, and tells other abbots whose boat to ask for.
endings.reward: 600 d; flag bk_carried; standing with churches along the Rhine and Seine; monks in other ports begin to ask for you by name

endings.how: The gatherings were lost to water or thieves on the way.
endings.text: A year of four scribes' work is gone. Hilduin does not shout. He has the loss reckoned in pennies and the reckoning sent after you.
endings.reward: flag bk_lost; a debt of 360 d to the abbey; the standing order ends; Hilduin's feeling falls to wary

endings.how: You sold the skins to Saint Germain's cellarer instead.
endings.text: Frotbald pays a little more and says nothing at all, with great satisfaction. At the fair the monk of Saint-Denis passes your booth without looking.
endings.reward: a better price once; Frotbald's feeling rises and the Saint-Germain errands open sooner; no standing order from Saint-Denis that year

stories.reward: A standing order that pays every October, the right to read and copy in the abbey, and a name among the monks of two rivers.

stories.title: Four pennies a head
stories.summary: Forty years after King Pippin struck it down, the count's man still stands at the fair asking four pennies a head from strangers who do not know better. What a merchant does about it sets him with the abbey or with the count.
stories.picture: Two tables side by side on a muddy river bank: at one a small sunburnt man with a long tally stick, at the other a spearman with an open hand, and a merchant between them with four crewmen behind him.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and month = 10 and year < 812
beats.text: Two tables at the landing. Dominicus takes the saint's toll on the boat and the cargo. A man of the count's, a little apart, asks four pennies for each free man aboard, as his fathers did.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and month = 10 and year < 812
beats.text: An English shipman ahead of you has a slave at the oar. The count's man makes the slave swear before witnesses that he is one, and then takes five pennies: one more than for a free man.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year < 807
beats.text: Abbot Fardulf will have King Pippin's judgment read to you from the abbey's chest: the merchants were staying away, and the king ended the tax. He asks whether you would say what you saw before the count's court.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year < 812
beats.text: The count's court sits in the yard. The law-finders hear the abbey's man, the count's man and a stranger from the sea. The count listens with his arms folded.

beats.when: year < 812
beats.text: Angilwin has heard of the count's man at the fair from every boat that comes down. He says the king's toll he takes is written, and that a toll nobody will write down is a different thing.

beats.when: year < 812
beats.text: Meginbert can say King Pippin's judgment nearly by heart, though it is the other abbey's. He says it for a cup of wine, and adds that Saint Germain's men never paid the head-penny either.

endings.how: You told the court what was asked of you at the landing.
endings.text: The law-finders find for the saint, as they did for his grandfathers. The count's man is gone from the landing for a few years. The count knows your face now, and not kindly.
endings.reward: the freedom of the fair (unlock_charter_parisius) for three fairs: no toll at Parisius while it lasts; Dominicus and Fardulf are friends; Stephen's feeling falls to cool

endings.how: You paid the saint's toll and the count's four pennies a head and said nothing.
endings.text: Sixteen pennies poorer. The count's man nods to you each year after, and once, when you are in a hurry, your boat is not searched.
endings.reward: Stephen's feeling rises; one lawsuit in the count's court goes easier; Dominicus says 'four heads' a little louder than he needs to

endings.how: You said at the landing, before everyone, that King Pippin struck the tax down.
endings.text: The count's man goes red and the queue behind you laughs. Dominicus waves you through and tells the story at his aunt's table for ten years.
endings.reward: no head-penny that year; a bench at the house by the Little Bridge (parisius.ermentruds_bench); the count's man remembers

stories.reward: The freedom of the fair for three years, or the count's quiet favour: not both.

stories.title: The fleet at the fair
stories.summary: From 845 the Northmen's ships come up the Seine as they come up the Rhine. The fair's silver goes to buy them off, the city burns twice, the abbey walls itself in, and a merchant must choose each time between standing, selling and running.
stories.picture: A wide river bend in winter mist seen from a low boat: far astern a line of long ships with many oars, ahead a timber bridge and an island wall with men on it.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 845 and year < 857
beats.text: A thin fair. Seven thousand pounds of silver went down the river at Easter, and the abbeys' plate went into the scales with it. Sellers want coin and nobody has it. A man with wine to give on trust can name his terms.

beats.when: year >= 845 and year < 887
beats.text: At the tide's head you see or hear of sails at the river mouth before any rider has brought word up. It is three days by water to Parisius, less for a small boat rowed hard. (Bringing the word sets df_warned.)

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 861 and year < 869
beats.text: Hildegaud tells how the merchants fled up the river in the winter the city burned, and how they were caught. He has a plan for next time and needs a second boat in it.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 865 and year < 867
beats.text: Northmen hold the island opposite the landing. Two hundred went up to the city for wine and found none. The law forbids selling them mail, weapons and horses on pain of death. It does not name wine.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year = 866
beats.text: The king's men go from boat to boat taking a tenth of all that a merchant is seen to have, toward four thousand pounds. They will take it in wine.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 869 and year < 885
beats.text: The abbey stands inside a new bank and wall with two wet ditches, and the fair is held within. The provost is selling stretches of wall to keep: a merchant who pays for one may store behind it.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 885 and year < 887
beats.text: The great fleet lies below the bridge and nothing passes. From the wall a young monk asks who you are and where you stood. The count needs grain brought in from above and word carried out.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and year >= 911 and year < 923
beats.text: A very big old Northman with a new cross sits in the count's yard with a clerk beside him: Rollo of Rotomagus, come up to speak with Count Robert. He asks you, through the clerk, what toll you paid at his town. The count is listening for the answer too.

beats.when: year >= 842 and year < 846
beats.text: The bank on the Canche has already learned what a fleet costs. Its people say: pay early, and do not wait to ask the king.

beats.when: year >= 843 and year < 846
beats.text: At the Loire they count who is missing since Saint John's day. A boat from the Seine is asked whether Paris has walls, and whether anyone stands on them.

endings.how: You brought warning, paid the tenth openly, or carried grain in during the siege.
endings.text: The house has a stretch of the saint's wall and a place behind it. Abbo asks where you stood, and for once has an answer to write down.
endings.reward: flag df_warned; flag parisius_stood; your stretch of the wall (parisius.work.wall_share) at half its cost; goods stored at Saint-Denis are safe in a raid year; high standing in Neustria

endings.how: You sold wine to the Northmen's camp.
endings.text: They pay in hacked silver by weight, more than the fair ever did, and remember a merchant who came unarmed. The monks remember too.
endings.reward: about twice a fair's profit; flag parisius_sold_island: Northmen on the Seine and Rollo's toll men at Rotomagus let the house pass easily; standing with the churches here falls; Dominicus's heirs count your casks twice

endings.how: You went with Hildegaud up the river with the cargo and lay hidden.
endings.text: You kept the boat, the casks and your skin, and were seen to have very little when the king's men came. Nobody thanks you and nobody blames you.
endings.reward: the cargo kept untaxed; Hildegaud a fast friend and partner: he holds casks for the house in the upper river landings; no standing gained

stories.reward: A place behind the saint's wall, or the Northmen's silver and an easy passage at Rotomagus, or simply the cargo kept.

stories.title: Pepper at the fair
stories.summary: Four Latin riddles, had in four ports, name the four things on a lord's table: salt, the wine cask, the glass cup and pepper. Whoever brings all four answers to the fair of Saint Denis is paid for them by the abbey, which likes a merchant who can think.
stories.picture: A monk at the abbey's booth holding up four fingers, on the trestle before him a dish of salt, a small cask, a green glass cup and a little heap of black peppercorns.

beats.when: year >= 793
beats.text: A monk on his abbey's business has Aldhelm's riddle of salt and will sell a copy. The answer wakes at a salt market.

beats.when: year >= 793
beats.text: At the salt pans the salt brother has the riddle of the wine cask, who lets strangers drink from her belly.

beats.when: year >= 793
beats.text: A Frisian wine shipper at Mogontia has the riddle of the cup that men kiss.

beats.when: year >= 793
beats.text: A dealer in Rhenish glass at Cologne has the last: black outside, wrinkled, and a burning inside. What it names is the dearest thing in any spice chest.

beats.when: moored and port.id = parisius and month = 10 and chest.riddles_solved >= 4
beats.text: At the abbey's booth the cellarer asks what a lord's table needs, in order. Four answers. He writes on a strip of parchment, loses it, writes another, and has that one sealed.

beats.when: year >= 836
beats.text: After the monks leave the salt island the cask riddle is kept at the Loire city, behind a tally board in the salt shed.

endings.how: You gave all four answers at the fair.
endings.text: For three fairs nobody but your house may sell pepper at Saint Denis. Dominicus turns a Greek away from the landing with real pleasure.
endings.reward: riddle reward rw_right_pepper: the sole right to sell pepper at the fair for three years

endings.how: You came to the fair with the set unfinished.
endings.text: The cellarer shakes his head, and then tells you quietly what will be short at the fair this year.
endings.reward: riddle reward rw_tip_parisius: every price at Parisius is sure for the day

endings.how: You sold the four answers to an English merchant in the ale-house.
endings.text: He takes the right and you take his silver. Ermentrud says you sold a cow for a cheese, and gives you the eel anyway.
endings.reward: 120 d at once; no right; the Englishman owes the house a favour at Hamwic

stories.reward: The sole right to sell pepper at the fair of Saint Denis for three years.

works.name: A booth at the fair
works.what: A standing booth of oak posts and wattle on the fair ground, kept for the house from year to year, with a locked chest sunk under the trestle.
works.needs: The abbot's leave, for the ground is the saint's: a gift, or the abbey's goodwill from the hungry years. Two pennies a year for the pitch.
works.gives: At the fair you sell from your own booth: buyers come to you, the market panel shows more buyers and better prices for cloth and wool, and unsold goods can stay locked there until Saint Andrew's.
works.picture: A booth of posts and woven hazel with a hide roof, bolts of cloth on its trestle, an abbey church behind and a crowd in front.
works.source: story/works_793.json fair_booth; later the fair's stalls stood in the graveyard at two pennies a pitch (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Saint-Denis fair)

works.name: A sunk cellar on the island
works.what: A cellar dug and stone-lined under a house by the Little Bridge, cool in summer and above the usual floods, for forty casks.
works.needs: A place in the house by the Little Bridge (Ermentrud's goodwill, or her heirs'), and a dry autumn for the digging.
works.gives: Buy the new wine at the vintage when it is cheapest and keep it until Lent or the next fair, when it is dear; casks in the cellar do not spoil. Lost if the city burns (857, 861) unless the house stood with the city.
works.picture: Stone steps going down into the dark under a timber house, a row of casks on their sides, a woman with a lamp and a ring of keys.
works.source: story/works_793.json cellar; wine as the trade of the place (Tardif no. 55); the fires of 856-857 and 861 (Annales Bertiniani)

works.name: An oven for the hospice
works.what: A second bread oven of stone and clay built against the hospice at the abbey gate, and a year's wood for it.
works.needs: A hungry year (793-794, 805-807, or any later famine), and the porter's word that it is wanted.
works.gives: The gate feeds more, and the monks pray for the house by name: standing with the church in Neustria rises each hungry year for as long as the oven stands; lodging and healing at the hospice cost the house nothing.
works.picture: Monks and a mason building a domed clay oven against a stone wall, thin people watching from where they sit, the first smoke rising.
works.source: story/works_793.json hospice; the abbey's bakery and the hospice at the gate (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, royal abbey); the spine's thread hungry_years

works.name: Your stretch of the saint's wall
works.what: Twenty paces of the bank, timber wall and ditch round Saint-Denis, kept in repair at the house's cost, with a store built against the inside of it.
works.needs: The provost's leave, and the house known at the abbey. Half the cost if the house stood with the city when the fleets came.
works.gives: Goods stored at Saint-Denis are safe in a raid year, and the house may trade at the fair when it is held inside the wall. Upkeep each winter.
works.picture: A raw earth bank with a wall of upright timbers on top and a wide wet ditch before it, men tamping clay, an abbey roof behind.
works.source: story/works_793.json wall_share; the castellum of 869, of wood and stone, about eight hectares, with a double ditch fed by the Croult (Annales Bertiniani 869; archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, fortification). That laymen kept stretches of it is the game's (?)

works.name: A roof for the church on the hill
works.what: Oak and tiles for the burned church of the Holy Apostles, where King Clovis and the holy woman Genevieve lie open to the rain.
works.needs: The church burned (after 28 December 856); timber rafted down from above the city.
works.gives: The house is named at Genevieve's tomb each third of January; standing in the city rises; the city's merchants treat the house as one of their own, and Hildegaud's kin stand surety for it once.
works.picture: A roofless stone church on a hilltop above a river and an island city, charred beams against the sky, carpenters raising the first new rafter.
works.source: story/works_793.json church_rebuilt; the church of Saint Peter and Saint Genevieve burned in 856-857 (Annales Bertiniani 857; fr.wikipedia, Abbaye Sainte-Geneviève de Paris). When and by whom it was mended is not recorded (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter, or hired with her crew by the trip
ships.note: The wine goes down the Seine in flat-bottomed barges and the cloth comes up in them, hauled against the stream. The wrights on the right bank build little else.
ships.picture: A long flat barge low in green-brown water under two rows of casks, a man at a steering sweep, an island wall behind.
ships.source: the charters say only 'boats' (Tardif no. 55); Design/content/ships.md and story/ships_793.json for the type. The yard is invented

ships.note: Every house on the island has one: to cross when the bridge is crowded, to reach a boat lying off, and in a bad year to be gone before morning.
ships.picture: A small flat-ended plank boat tied under a timber bridge, one pole and one bailer in it.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_skiff_punt; the city's merchants with their own boats (Annales Bertiniani 861)

ships.how: bought second-hand at the fair's end
ships.note: Fishermen and ferrymen from the lower river sell a boat at Saint Andrew's rather than row her home empty against the winter stream.
ships.picture: A small open working boat with four oars drawn up on river mud among bare willows, a man counting pennies beside her.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md (the small working boat of the Frankish rivers and coast); the sale at the fair's end is invented

ships.how: lent by an abbey to a merchant who carries for it
ships.note: Saint-Denis and Saint-Germain both keep river ships for their own wine and their abbots. She is the saint's, not yours: his goods go toll-free in her wherever his charter runs, and yours may ride beside them.
ships.picture: A broad river ship with a small cabin aft and a cross painted on her bow, rowed by eight men, casks amidships under an awning.
