ships.source: story/ships_793.json (built_at parisius; how_had: reward) and story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_estate_ship; Saint-Germain's traders free of toll, 779 (Tardif no. 81)

ships.how: bought second-hand from a Frisian or English master at the fair
ships.note: Not built here. But the fair brings sea keels up the river, and now and then a master dies of the autumn fever or cannot pay his lodging, and his ship is sold where she lies.
ships.picture: A round-bellied sea ship with one mast lying at a river bank far from the sea, her sail unbent, a woman in mourning standing by her.
ships.source: Saxon (English) and Frisian merchants at the fair (Tardif nos. 44, 55); the sale is invented, and agrees with the chain wine_fleet's last card (end_own)

sayings.text: They come to buy wine in the ports and on the rivers.
sayings.source: King Pippin's judgment for Saint-Denis, 8 July 753 (Tardif no. 55), in the dossier's rendering of the Latin

sayings.text: A free man swears and pays four. A slave swears and pays five. Honesty has always cost a little extra.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the head-penny of the judgment of 753

sayings.text: What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed and when I am on horseback I cannot shield myself with them against wind and rain.
sayings.source: King Charles on the short Frisian cloaks, Notker of Saint-Gall, Deeds of Charles I.34, in the translation of A. J. Grant, Early Lives of Charlemagne (London, Chatto and Windus 1907), p. 104, word for word (Grant leaves out the king's third complaint)

sayings.text: Two hundred Northmen came to Paris for wine and found none. It is the only thing they ever left as they found it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Annales Bertiniani 865; said from 865

sayings.text: I should deserve that my head be cut off and thrown to the dogs.
sayings.source: Sigfred the Dane to Bishop Gozlin at Paris, Abbo, Bella Parisiacae urbis I, as given in F. A. Ogg, A Source Book of Mediaeval History (1907); said from 886 (Design/content/peoples/frankish.md)

sayings.text: A dog's arse in your nose.
sayings.source: 'Undes ars in tine naso', an insult in a traveller's phrase list of the 10th or 11th century kept at Paris (the Paris Conversations), our rendering (?); said from about 950

sayings.text: The king wished to lie at Saint-Denis. He lies at Nantua, in a barrel. Man asks; the road answers.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Annales Bertiniani 877; said from 877

sayings.text: Denis sells the wine and Martin drinks it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the fair opens on Saint Denis's day (9 October) and the new wine is drunk at Martinmas (11 November)

sayings.text: This year the Seine stood so hard that carts went over it for thirty days.
sayings.source: in the Chronicle's manner, from Annales regni Francorum 821 (chronicle_793.json 821-winter-rivers-frozen); said from 822

sayings.text: The skin is hairy, the ink is thin, the light is going. Saint Denis, lend me your head: mine aches.
sayings.source: a scribe's complaint invented in the manner of the monks' marginal notes; the saint carries his head only from Hilduin's Passion of 835-840, so said from 840

easter_eggs.text: A monk shows you a description of the church: 245 feet long, 101 windows, doors of gold, silver and ivory. A brother from Tours, reading over his shoulder, says his own church's description has the same words and smaller numbers.
easter_eggs.source: the text of 799 is copied from a description of Saint Martin's at Tours, 160 feet and 55 windows there (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Description of the basilica in 799); seen from 799

easter_eggs.text: Workmen clearing the trench of the abbey's water channel turn up a small plate of lead with a penny's face struck into it several times, crooked: King Pippin's. Somebody tried his die on it before he spoiled silver. They throw it back.
easter_eggs.source: a lead trial piece for a penny of Pippin, found in the aqueduct trench: the abbey had a mint (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, coin die trial piece)

easter_eggs.text: In the stone hall north of the church a floor has been dug and badly put back. A lay brother says five chests and a barrel went into the ground there in one night, and the men who buried them did not all come home.
easter_eggs.source: five chests and a barrel buried in haste in a room of the stone hall (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Carolingian chest). When, and by whom, is not known (?): the game shows it after 845

easter_eggs.text: A boy in a monk's habit, perhaps fourteen, well born by his speech, asks you gravely whether the sea is really salt all the way down. His name is Hunus. He will not see seventeen.
easter_eggs.source: the boy monk Hunus, noble, dead at sixteen between 838 and 845, known from his epitaph (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Hunus). His question is invented; met 836-843

easter_eggs.text: You drop a penny of Dorestad in the fair's mud and cannot find it. It will be found, with one of Quentovic and an older small thick coin of the Frisians, in eleven hundred years.
easter_eggs.source: pennies of Dorestad and of Quentovic and a sceat found in the digs at Saint-Denis (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Saint-Denis fair)

easter_eggs.text: Ask in 793 how the saint died and you are told: a bishop, beheaded with two companions on the hill. Ask after 840 and you are told he picked up his head and walked here with it. Nobody remarks on the change.
easter_eggs.source: that Denis carried his head from Montmartre is first written in Hilduin's Passion of 835-840 (fr.wikipedia, Denis de Paris)

easter_eggs.text: In the abbey's chest is a charter of King Offa giving the saint ground 'in the port called Lundenuuic'. The ink is fresher than the date. The treasurer does not like it looked at closely.
easter_eggs.source: the charter of Offa for Saint-Denis dated 790 (Sawyer 133) is a forgery, perhaps on a true base: https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/133.html. When it was made is not known (?)

easter_eggs.text: The shoemakers inside the saint's wall throw their offcuts into the ditch: toe-pieces, thongs, a child's sole cut wrong. The rule gives each monk two pairs of shoes; the ditch gets the rest.
easter_eggs.source: a shoemakers' shop in the castellum named in 898, its offcuts found in the ditch; two pairs of shoes by the rule of 816-817 (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/saint-denis, Carolingian shoemaker); seen from about 890

easter_eggs.text: On the left-bank hill a priest will show you, for a penny for the lamp, the grave of the first Christian king of the Franks, and beside it the grave of the woman whose prayers, they say, turned Attila from the city.
easter_eggs.source: the Holy Apostles, with the graves of Clovis, Clotilde and Genevieve (fr.wikipedia, Abbaye Sainte-Geneviève de Paris; Geneviève de Paris). The church burned in 856-857

easter_eggs.text: Men digging by the bishop's church say there are carved stones deep under it with boatmen on them, and a god with horns. The clerks say it is nothing and to fill the hole.
easter_eggs.source: the pillar of the Roman boatmen of Paris, found under the cathedral in 1711: from memory, unchecked (?). That anyone saw it in these years is invented

unlocks.what: The freedom of the fair of Saint Denis
unlocks.how: Bear witness for the abbey in the count's court (the story parisius.four_pennies), or be well regarded here and ask the abbot on the saint's day.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_charter_parisius: no toll at Parisius during the fair. It is the saint's freedom, not yours: it lapses if captives or arms are carried under it

unlocks.how: Carry for Frotbald three times between the Seine and the Rhine mouth and lose nothing.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_charter_dorestad, unlock_charter_quentovic and unlock_charter_rotomagus: with the abbey's goods aboard you show the charter of 779 and pay no toll there; each year before the fair the abbey is owed its cloth and wax

unlocks.what: The loan of an abbey's river ship
unlocks.how: Hold a standing order from either abbey for two years running.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_estate_ship: the ship class river_estate_ship, lent; she goes back when the abbot dies or the house fails him

unlocks.what: The abbey's standing order for parchment
unlocks.how: Bring dry parchment to Saint-Denis at two fairs before 842 (the story parisius.skins_for_the_saint).
unlocks.gives: flag bk_parchment: a commission each October; act:read_text and act:copy_text at Saint-Denis

unlocks.what: A bench at the house by the Little Bridge
unlocks.how: Lodge there at three fairs and pay what you owe; or make the count's man look a fool at the landing.
unlocks.gives: Lodging at Parisius costs nothing; act:rumours there gives the newest word of the fair first; Ermentrud nurses a sick man of the crew for nothing. Her heirs keep the bench for yours

unlocks.how: Declare truly at the landing at three fairs.
unlocks.gives: Paying the toll at the saint's landing takes no time, and Dominicus sends word down to Rotomagus so that the toll man there is easier on the house

unlocks.what: The sole right to sell pepper at the fair
unlocks.how: Bring the four answers of the riddle set salt_to_pepper to the abbey's booth in October.
unlocks.gives: riddle reward rw_right_pepper, for three fairs

unlocks.what: A place behind the saint's wall
unlocks.how: From 869: stand with the city in a raid year, or pay for a stretch of the wall.
unlocks.gives: flag parisius_stood: goods left at Saint-Denis are not lost in a raid; the fair is open to the house when it is held inside the stronghold
